language.name: Spanish
features: Subject pronouns are often omitted because the verb identifies the person.
Formal usted takes third-person singular verb endings.
Negate a clause with no immediately before its finite verb group.
Written questions start with ¿ and end with ?.
Poder and querer take an infinitive to express ability and desire.

lessons.title: First words
lessons.goal: Start and end a simple interaction
lessons.introduction: A few social expressions are conventional, not assembled by grammar. Learn these short forms as complete units.

notes.explanation: These are social expressions to remember as whole units. They are useful before you learn any verb endings.
notes.detail: This guide chooses formal usted for requests to strangers. Spanish-speaking regions differ in how often formal address is expected.
notes.caution: Use gracias for thanks and de nada as a conventional reply; there is no need to translate them word by word.

lessons.title: Needs and possession
lessons.goal: Say what you need or already have
lessons.introduction: A verb plus an interchangeable noun phrase gives you a whole family of useful statements.

notes.explanation: Necesito means I need; tengo means I have. Spanish often omits yo because the verb ending already identifies the speaker.
notes.detail: Learn un billete, un café, agua, and ayuda. Direct objects do not normally require a German-style case ending.
notes.caution: Do not add yo before every verb. It is optional for emphasis but usually unnecessary here.

lessons.title: What you would like
lessons.introduction: One courteous construction works with many objects. Substitute the thing you want instead of memorizing an order.

notes.explanation: Quisiera is a polite conventional form for “I would like.” It is well suited to everyday requests.
notes.detail: A café is un café; water is agua. The formal question ¿Quisiera un café? is an offer to the listener.
notes.caution: Quiero is valid “I want,” but quisiera sounds less abrupt in service situations.

lessons.title: Yes/no questions
lessons.introduction: A question changes the form of a whole clause. The same mechanism works with several verbs.

notes.explanation: Spanish often forms a yes/no question without adding a helper word. In writing, the opening ¿ marks the question.
notes.detail: With usted the finite verb is third-person singular: ¿Tiene tiempo? The speaker’s own verb forms end differently: tengo, necesito.
notes.caution: Spanish subject pronouns are often omitted; including usted can add emphasis, but is not always required.

lessons.title: Ask for help
lessons.introduction: A question, a modal verb and an action can be combined. Change the recipient or action to make a new request.

notes.explanation: Puede means formal “you can.” A second verb follows in the infinitive: ayudarme, repetirme or repetir esto.
notes.detail: In ayudarme the object me is attached to the infinitive. With a simple finite verb it goes before: me ayuda.
notes.caution: ¿Usted puede ayudarme? is correct, but many speakers would naturally omit usted.

lessons.title: When you do not understand
lessons.introduction: Say what you cannot understand and ask for clarification instead of trying to guess.

notes.recipe: No + verb + rest. / Hable más despacio, por favor.
notes.explanation: Negation is direct: put no before the verb. Memorize the slower-speech request as a polite fixed expression.
notes.detail: No entiendo esto and no hablo español apply the same negative rule to different predicates.
notes.caution: No usually stays immediately before the verb (or an attached pronoun group).

lessons.title: Places and directions
lessons.goal: Find a place and say where you are going
lessons.introduction: The place is a slot. Its preposition and article are handled by the language, not by you inventing a new sentence.

notes.explanation: ¿Dónde está …? asks for a location. Voy a … says where you are going.
notes.detail: Learn la estación, el hotel, el baño and a casa as complete chunks. Al combines a + el.
notes.caution: The article changes by noun: la estación, but el hotel and el baño.

lessons.title: Buying and paying
lessons.goal: Ask a price and pay for something
lessons.introduction: Combine price questions, purchasing and payment methods. Only the useful noun or payment method changes.

notes.explanation: ¿Cuánto cuesta …? asks for a price. Puedo pagar asks whether you can pay in a particular way.
notes.detail: Con tarjeta is by card; en efectivo is in cash. After puedo, use the infinitive pagar.
notes.caution: Use cuesta for a single item. Plural prices would require cuestan and are outside this starter pattern.

examples.english: How much does a ticket cost?
How much does a coffee cost?
I want to buy a ticket.
I want to buy a coffee.

lessons.title: Today and tomorrow
lessons.goal: Situate a simple statement in time
lessons.introduction: Adding a time expression makes ordinary statements useful for near-future plans, without learning new tenses first.

notes.explanation: Hoy means today and mañana means tomorrow. You can place these at the end of a short present-tense clause.
notes.detail: Present tense plus mañana is frequently enough for a clear near-future plan in the restricted contexts taught here.
notes.caution: Mañana can also refer to morning; the surrounding words determine the meaning.

examples.english: I go to the hotel tomorrow.
I go to the station tomorrow.
I want to buy a ticket today.

lessons.title: Say no and set limits
lessons.goal: Turn a positive sentence into a negative one
lessons.introduction: Negation is an operator: it changes the meaning of a clause, while each language decides where its negative words go.

notes.explanation: No goes immediately before the conjugated verb. The rest of the sentence can usually stay as it was.
notes.detail: Compare tengo un billete with no tengo un billete, and puedo ir with no puedo ir.
notes.caution: Do not put no after the finite verb as in English “do not.”

examples.english: I do not have a ticket.
I cannot go to the station today.
examples.target: No puedo ir a la estación hoy.

lessons.title: Put the blocks together
lessons.introduction: Put a greeting, a question, a need and a request into separate short sentences. Complexity is optional.

notes.explanation: Build a practical interaction from small complete sentences: greet, ask, clarify, and thank the other person.
notes.detail: Spanish lets you omit many subject pronouns, so even longer exchanges can remain quite compact.
notes.caution: There are major regional varieties of Spanish; this guide chooses one consistent European reference variety.

examples.english: How much does a ticket cost?
